title: Book 5 — Calypso—Odysseus reaches Scheria on a raft
paragraphs: As Dawn rose from her bed beside Tithonus, bringing light to both mortals and immortals, the gods gathered in council with Zeus, lord of thunder and their king. There Athena began telling them of Odysseus's many sufferings, for she pitied him trapped in the nymph Calypso's home.

"Father Zeus," she said, "and all you other gods who live in eternal bliss, I hope there's never again such a thing as a kind and fair-minded ruler, nor one who governs justly. I hope they'll all be cruel and unjust from now on, since not one of his subjects remembers Odysseus, who ruled them like a father. There he lies in great pain on an island where the nymph Calypso lives, and she won't let him go. He can't get back to his own country because he has no ships or sailors to carry him across the sea. And now wicked men are trying to murder his only son Telemachus, who's returning from Pylos and Sparta where he went seeking news of his father."

"What are you talking about, my dear?" her father replied. "Didn't you send him there yourself because you thought it would help Odysseus get home and punish the suitors? Besides, you're perfectly able to protect Telemachus and see him safely home, while the suitors will have to scurry back without killing him."

After speaking, he turned to his son Hermes. "Hermes, you are our messenger, so go tell Calypso that we've decided poor Odysseus must return home. He won't be escorted by gods or men, but after twenty perilous days on a raft he'll reach fertile Scheria, land of the Phaeacians, who are close to the gods and will honor him as one of us. They'll send him home in a ship and give him more bronze, gold, and clothing than he would have brought back from Troy if he'd had all his prize money and returned without disaster. This is how we've decided he shall return to his country and friends."

Zeus spoke, and Hermes the guide and guardian, slayer of Argus, obeyed. He immediately bound on his glittering golden sandals that let him fly like wind over land and sea. He took his wand that puts men to sleep or wakes them as he pleases, and holding it flew over Pieria, then swooped down through the sky until he reached sea level, skimming the waves like a cormorant fishing every corner of the ocean, drenching its thick feathers in spray. He flew over many weary waves until he finally reached the island that was his destination, left the sea, and went overland to the cave where the nymph Calypso lived.

He found her at home. A large fire burned on the hearth, and the fragrant smoke of burning cedar and sandalwood could be smelled from far away. She was busy at her loom, shooting her golden shuttle through the warp and singing beautifully. Around her cave grew a thick wood of alder, poplar, and sweet-smelling cypress trees where all kinds of birds had built their nests—owls, hawks, and chattering sea-crows that make their living from the waters. A vine heavy with grapes grew luxuriously around the cave's mouth. Four streams of water flowed in channels cut close together, winding here and there to water beds of violets and lush plants. Even a god couldn't help being charmed by such a lovely spot, so Hermes stood still and admired it before going inside the cave.

Calypso recognized him at once—the gods all know each other no matter how far apart they live—but Odysseus wasn't there. He was on the seashore as usual, staring at the barren ocean with tears in his eyes, groaning and breaking his heart with sorrow. Calypso offered Hermes a seat and said, "Why have you come to see me, Hermes—honored and always welcome—since you don't visit me often? Tell me what you want. I'll do it at once if I can and if it's possible. But come inside and let me offer you refreshment."
As she spoke, she drew up a table loaded with ambrosia and mixed him red nectar. Hermes ate and drank until he was satisfied, then said:

"We're speaking as god to goddess, and you ask why I've come, so I'll tell you truthfully as you wish. Zeus sent me—it wasn't my idea. Who would want to come all this way across the sea where there are no cities full of people to offer sacrifices or choice offerings? But I had to come, since none of us other gods can cross Zeus or disobey his orders. He says you have here the most cursed of all those who fought nine years before King Priam's city and sailed home in the tenth year after sacking it. On their way home they offended Athena, who raised wind and waves against them so that all his brave companions died, and he alone was carried here by wind and tide. Zeus says you must let this man go at once, for it's decreed that he won't die here far from his people, but will return to his house and country to see his friends again."

Calypso trembled with rage at these words. "You gods should be ashamed of yourselves," she cried. "You're always jealous and hate seeing a goddess fall for a mortal man and live with him openly. When rosy-fingered Dawn loved Orion, you precious gods were furious until Artemis killed him in Ortygia. When Demeter fell in love with Iasion and lay with him in a thrice-plowed field, Zeus heard about it quickly and killed Iasion with his thunderbolts. Now you're angry with me because I have a man here. I found the poor creature sitting alone on a ship's keel after Zeus struck his ship with lightning and sunk it mid-ocean, drowning his entire crew while he was driven by wind and waves to my island. I grew fond of him and cared for him, planning to make him immortal so he'd never age. But I can't cross Zeus or frustrate his plans. So if he insists, let the man sail beyond the seas again. But I can't send him anywhere myself since I have no ships or men to take him. Still, I'll gladly give him good advice that will help him reach his own country safely."
"Then send him away," said Hermes, "or Zeus will be angry and punish you."

With that he left, and Calypso went to find Odysseus, having heard Zeus's message. She found him sitting on the beach with his eyes full of tears, dying of homesickness. He'd grown tired of Calypso, and though he was forced to sleep with her in the cave at night, it was she, not he, who wanted it. During the day he spent time on the rocks and seashore, weeping and crying out in despair, always staring at the sea. Calypso approached him and said:

"Poor man, don't stay here grieving and wasting your life any longer. I'm going to send you away of my own free will. Go cut some logs and build yourself a large raft with a deck that can carry you safely across the sea. I'll put bread, wine, and water aboard to keep you from starving. I'll also give you clothes and send you a fair wind to take you home, if the gods in heaven will it—for they know more about these things and can manage them better than I can."

Odysseus shuddered at her words. "Now goddess," he answered, "there's something behind all this. You can't really mean to help me home when you tell me to do something as terrible as put to sea on a raft. Not even a well-built ship with fair wind would attempt such a distant voyage. Nothing you say or do will make me board a raft unless you first solemnly swear you mean me no harm."

Calypso smiled at this and stroked him with her hand. "You're very clever," she said, "but you're quite wrong here. Let heaven above and earth below witness, along with the waters of the river Styx—the most solemn oath a blessed god can take—that I mean you no harm and am only advising you to do exactly what I'd do in your place. I'm being completely honest with you. My heart isn't made of iron, and I feel very sorry for you."

After speaking she led the way quickly, and Odysseus followed until they reached Calypso's cave, where Odysseus took the seat Hermes had just left. Calypso set mortal food and drink before him while her maids brought ambrosia and nectar for herself. They ate the good food set before them. When they'd satisfied themselves, Calypso spoke:

"Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, so you want to go straight home to your own land? Good luck to you, but if you only knew how much suffering awaits you before you reach your country, you'd stay here, keep house with me, and let me make you immortal, no matter how anxious you are to see this wife you think about constantly. Yet I flatter myself that I'm no less tall or beautiful than she is, for no mortal woman should compare in beauty with an immortal."

"Goddess," replied Odysseus, "don't be angry about this. I know perfectly well that my wife Penelope is nothing like as tall or beautiful as you. She's only a woman, while you're an immortal. Still, I want to get home and can think of nothing else. If some god wrecks me at sea, I'll bear it and make the best of it. I've already had endless trouble on land and sea, so let this be added to the rest."
Soon the sun set and darkness fell, so the pair retired to the inner part of the cave and went to bed.

When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, Odysseus put on his shirt and cloak while the goddess wore a dress of light, gossamer fabric, very fine and graceful, with a beautiful golden belt around her waist and a veil over her head. She immediately began thinking how to speed Odysseus on his way. She gave him a great bronze ax that fit his hands perfectly—sharpened on both sides with a beautiful olive-wood handle fitted firmly to it. She also gave him a sharp adze and led him to the far end of the island where the largest trees grew—alder, poplar, and pine reaching to the sky, very dry and well-seasoned to sail lightly on the water. After showing him the best trees, Calypso went home, leaving him to cut them, which he quickly finished. He cut down twenty trees and smoothed them with the adze, squaring them properly with good workmanship. Meanwhile Calypso returned with augers, so he drilled holes and fitted the timbers together with bolts and rivets. He made the raft as broad as a skilled shipwright makes a large vessel's beam, fixed a deck on top of the ribs, and ran a gunwale all around it. He also made a mast with a yardarm and a rudder to steer with. He fenced the raft with wicker hurdles as protection against waves, then threw on plenty of wood. Soon Calypso brought him linen for sails, and he made these excellently too, securing them with braces and sheets. Finally, using levers, he dragged the raft into the water.

In four days he'd completed the whole job, and on the fifth Calypso sent him from the island after washing him and giving him clean clothes. She gave him a goatskin full of dark wine and another larger one of water. She also gave him a bag full of provisions with plenty of good meat. Moreover, she made the wind fair and warm for him, and Odysseus gladly spread his sail, sitting and skillfully guiding the raft with the rudder. He never closed his eyes but kept them fixed on the Pleiades, late-setting Boötes, and the Bear—which men also call the Wagon, which turns around in place facing Orion and alone never dips into Ocean's stream—for Calypso had told him to keep this on his left. For seventeen days he sailed over the sea, and on the eighteenth the dim outlines of mountains on the nearest part of the Phaeacian coast appeared, rising like a shield on the horizon.

But King Poseidon, returning from the Ethiopians, spotted Odysseus from far off, from the Solymi mountains. He could see him sailing on the sea, and it made him furious. He shook his head and muttered to himself, "Good heavens, so the gods have changed their minds about Odysseus while I was away in Ethiopia, and now he's close to the Phaeacian land where he's destined to escape the troubles that have befallen him. Still, he'll have plenty more hardship before he's done."

Then he gathered his clouds, grasped his trident, stirred up the sea, and roused every wind to fury until earth, sea, and sky were hidden in cloud and night sprang from the heavens. Winds from east, south, north, and west struck him all at once, raising a tremendous sea that made Odysseus's heart fail. "Alas," he said to himself in dismay, "what will become of me? I'm afraid Calypso was right when she said I'd have trouble at sea before getting home. It's all coming true. How dark Zeus is making heaven with his clouds, and what a sea the winds are raising from every direction at once. Now I'm sure to die. Blessed and thrice blessed were those Greeks who fell before Troy fighting for the sons of Atreus. I wish I'd been killed the day the Trojans pressed me so hard around dead Achilles' body, for then I'd have had proper burial and the Greeks would have honored my name. But now it seems I'll come to the most wretched end."

As he spoke a wave broke over him with such terrible force that the raft spun around and he was hurled far overboard. He lost hold of the steering oar, and the hurricane's force was so great it snapped the mast in half, sending both sail and yardarm into the sea. For a long time Odysseus was underwater, barely able to surface again because the clothes Calypso had given him weighed him down. But finally he got his head above water and spat out the bitter brine streaming down his face. Despite everything, he didn't lose sight of his raft but swam as fast as he could toward it, grabbed hold, and climbed back aboard to escape drowning. The sea tossed the raft about like autumn winds whirling thistledown on a road. It was as if the south, north, east, and west winds were all playing battledore and shuttlecock with it at once.

While he was in this plight, Ino, daughter of Cadmus, also called Leucothea, saw him. She'd once been mortal but had since been raised to marine goddess rank. Seeing Odysseus's great distress, she took pity on him and, rising like a seagull from the waves, perched on the raft.

"My poor good man," she said, "why is Poseidon so furiously angry with you? He's giving you great trouble, but for all his bluster he won't kill you. You seem sensible, so do as I tell you: strip off your clothes, leave your raft to drift before the wind, and swim to the Phaeacian coast where better luck awaits you. Here, take my veil and wrap it around your chest—it's enchanted, and you can't be harmed while wearing it. As soon as you touch land, take it off, throw it as far as you can back into the sea, and then go away." With these words she removed her veil and gave it to him, then dove down like a seagull and vanished beneath the dark blue waters.

But Odysseus didn't know what to think. "Alas," he said to himself in dismay, "this is probably just another god trying to trick me into ruin by telling me to abandon my raft. I won't do it now, since the land where she said I'd escape all troubles still seems far away. I know what I'll do—I'm sure it's best—whatever happens, I'll stick to the raft as long as its timbers hold together. But when the sea breaks it up, I'll swim for it. I don't see how I can do better than this."

While he was torn between choices, Poseidon sent a terrible great wave that seemed to rear above his head before breaking right over the raft, which went to pieces like dry chaff tossed by a whirlwind. Odysseus straddled one plank and rode it like a horse. He then stripped off the clothes Calypso had given him, bound Ino's veil under his arms, and plunged into the sea, intending to swim to shore. King Poseidon watched him do this and shook his head, muttering, "There now, swim around as best you can until you meet some well-off people. I don't think you'll be able to say I let you off too lightly." With that he whipped his horses and drove to Aegae where his palace stands.

But Athena resolved to help Odysseus, so she stopped all winds except one and made them lie still. She raised a good stiff north wind that would calm the waters until Odysseus reached the Phaeacian land where he'd be safe.

So he floated for two nights and two days in heavy swells with death staring him in the face. But when the third day dawned, the wind died and there was dead calm without even a breath of air stirring. As he rose on a swell he looked eagerly ahead and could see land quite near. Then, as children rejoice when their dear father begins recovering after long suffering from some illness sent by an angry spirit, but the gods deliver him from evil, so Odysseus was thankful to see land and trees again, and swam with all his strength to set foot on dry ground once more. But when he got within earshot, he began hearing surf thundering against rocks, for swells still broke against them with a terrific roar. Everything was shrouded in spray—there were no harbors where a ship might anchor, no shelter of any kind, only headlands, jagged rocks, and mountain tops.

Odysseus's heart began to fail him, and he said despairingly to himself, "Alas, Zeus has let me see land after swimming so far that I'd given up all hope, but I can find no landing place. The coast is rocky and surf-beaten, the rocks are smooth and rise straight from the sea with deep water right under them, so I can't climb out for lack of footholds. I'm afraid some great wave will lift me up and dash me against the rocks as I leave the water—which would be a sorry landing indeed. If I swim further looking for some sloping beach or harbor, a hurricane may carry me back out to sea against my will, or heaven may send some great sea monster to attack me, for Amphitrite breeds many such, and I know Poseidon is very angry with me."

While he was torn between choices, a wave caught him and hurled him with such force against the rocks that he would have been smashed to pieces if Athena hadn't shown him what to do. He grabbed the rock with both hands and clung to it, groaning with pain until the wave receded—so he was saved that time. But then the wave came again and carried him far back into the sea, tearing his hands as the suckers of an octopus are torn when someone pulls it from its bed with stones still clinging—so the rocks tore skin from his strong hands, and the wave dragged him deep underwater.

Here poor Odysseus would certainly have died despite his destiny if Athena hadn't helped him keep his wits. He swam back out to sea, beyond reach of the surf beating against the land, while looking toward shore to find some haven or spit that might deflect the waves. Swimming on, he came to a river mouth, which seemed the best place since there were no rocks and it offered shelter from the wind. He felt a current, so he prayed inwardly:

"Hear me, O King, whoever you are, and save me from sea-god Poseidon's anger, for I approach you as a suppliant. Anyone who has lost his way has a claim on the gods, so in my distress I draw near to your stream and grasp the knees of your river-godhead. Have mercy on me, O King, for I declare myself your suppliant."

Then the god stopped his current and stilled the waves, making all calm before him and bringing him safely into the river mouth. Here at last Odysseus's knees and strong hands failed him, for the sea had completely broken him. His whole body was swollen, and seawater poured from his mouth and nostrils like a river, so he could neither breathe nor speak, lying unconscious from sheer exhaustion. When he'd caught his breath and come to himself again, he took off the scarf Ino had given him and threw it back into the river's salt stream, where Ino received it in her hands from the wave that bore it to her. Then he left the river, lay down among the rushes, and kissed the bountiful earth.

"Alas," he cried to himself in dismay, "what will become of me, and how will this all end? If I stay here on the riverbank through the long night watches, I'm so exhausted that the bitter cold and damp may finish me—for toward sunrise there'll be a keen wind blowing from the river. But if I climb the hillside, find shelter in the woods, and sleep in some thicket, I may escape the cold and get a good night's rest, though some wild beast may take advantage of me and devour me."

In the end he decided it was best to head for the woods, and he found one on high ground not far from the water. There he crept beneath two olive shoots growing from a single trunk—one wild, the other grafted. No wind, however fierce, could break through the cover they provided, nor could sun's rays pierce them, nor rain get through them, so closely did they grow together. Odysseus crawled under these and began making himself a bed, for there was a great pile of dead leaves lying about—enough to cover two or three men even in harsh winter weather. He was glad to see this, so he lay down and heaped leaves all around him. Then, like someone who lives alone in the country, far from any neighbor, who buries a burning brand in ashes to preserve fire and avoid having to get light elsewhere, so Odysseus covered himself with leaves. And Athena poured sweet sleep upon his eyes, closed his eyelids, and made him forget all his sorrows.
